diagnosis: Adds both the numerators and the denominators together instead of keeping the common denominator.
rationale: The student computed 2+1=3 for the numerator and 5+5=10 for the denominator. A number line partitioned into fifths clearly demonstrates that adding fifths means hopping along fifths, leaving the denominator unchanged.

script.focus: The size of the units stays as sixths while counting hops.

intent: Demonstrate add on the number-line with values [3,2] (unit 1/6). Tutor points at: The size of the units stays as sixths while counting hops.

frames.caption: Start at 3/6. We are standing here; we have not hopped yet.
Hop 1 moves 1/6 forward and lands on 4/6. One hop is one sixth.
Hop 2 lands on 5/6. 2 hops, so 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. Every hop was one sixth; the size of the pieces never changed, only how many.

judgement.reasoning: The student erroneously adds denominators (2/5 + 1/5 = 3/10). The demo specifically illustrates adding fractions on a number line (3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6), explicitly pointing out that the unit size (sixths) stays constant and only the count changes. This switches from fraction bars to a number line model, is simpler since it is an ungraded worked demo, and directly addresses the misconception.
judgement.verdict: A teacher would definitely use this clear, worked visual demonstration to show why the denominator remains unchanged when adding fractions.
